events.title: All About my Mother (1999) on 35mm
events.description:
All About my Mother (Todo sobre mi madre), 1999, Spain/France

Pedro Almodóvar’s All About my Mother tells the story of how a woman (Cecilia Roth), struggling to get her life in order after her son’s (Eloy Azorín) death, is helped by a set of new friends. A landmark of queer cinema, with the director’s signature pallette of vivid colours and emotional intensity.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: The Smallest Shows on Earth
events.description:
A celebration of the little, lost, ‘fleapit’ cinemas of East London with social historian and Radio 4 presenter Alan Dein. Alan is a multi-award winning writer and broadcaster whose great grandparents were the proprietors of The Cable Picture Palace, a notorious ‘fleapit’ in Cable Street, hugely popular with the locals, but raised to the ground in 1941 during The Blitz.

Alan’s fascinating talk will include a screening of The Smallest Show on Earth (1957) starring Margaret Rutherford, Bernard Miles and Peter Sellers, accompanied by some theatrical surprises along the way.

events.title: Thunder Road (1958) on 35mm
events.description:
Director Arthur Ripley, and starring Robert Mitchum and Gene Barry. 35mm film presentation.

An American Southern Gothic film noir starring Robert Mitchum as a Tennessee moonshine driver. Out making dangerous high-speed deliveries, he is under pressure from gangsters wanting in on the action, and Treasury agents wanting him in jail.

Some fun facts. Mitchum gets a story credit – he was told by writer James Agee about an incident in which a driver transporting moonshine was said to have crashed to his death on Kingston Pike in Knoxville, Tennessee. The part of Mitchum’s son in the film was due to be played by Elvis Presley, and having been sent the screenplay by Mitchum, Elvis was keen, but Colonel Tom Parker demanded a ridiculously inflated fee for his client, and the part went to Mitchum’s son James. Bruce Springsteen says he was inspired to call his song Thunder Road after seeing a poster of the film – but he has not seen the film itself!

events.title: 80 Years of Martin and Lewis: Hollywood or Bust (1956)
events.description:
Martin and Lewis’s final film is also one of their funniest. Released six months after their infamous split, Hollywood or Bust (1956) marked their second collaboration with Cahiers-darling Frank Tashlin.

Lewis plays crazed cinephile Malcolm Smith who, after winning a shiny new car at a raffle, plans to drive to Hollywood to meet his beloved Anita Ekberg. When con artist Steve Wiley (Martin) claims the prize with a forged ticket, naive Malcolm is thrilled to have gained both a car and a friend. But as the pair set off for Hollywood, Steve bends over backwards to rid himself of his irritating new companion.

Even for those unfamiliar with Lewis’s work, his well-known (and oft-derided) acclaim in France endures. It was through this collaboration with Tashlin that Lewis first caught the attention of the French auteurists. Writing in Cahiers du Cinéma in July 1957, Jean-Luc Godard remarked:

“Frank Tashlin has not renovated the Hollywood comedy. He has done better. There is not a difference in degree between Hollywood or Bust and It Happened One Night, but a difference in kind. Tashlin, in other words, has not renewed but created. And henceforth, when you talk about a comedy, don’t say ‘It’s Chaplinesque’; say, loud and clear, ‘‘It’s Tashlinesque’.“

The film will be preceded by an introduction from I’ll Say She Is curator Charlotte Ross.

events.title: Italy Through its Cinema: Cinema Paradiso (1988)
events.description:
Cinema Paradiso (1988) Directed by Giuseppe Tornatore, and starring Philippe Noiret and Salvatore Cascio. 35mm Film Presentation (International version)

Filmmaker Salvatore Di Vita recalls his childhood friendship with projectionist Alfredo, whose guidance nurtured his love of cinema in a small Sicilian village.

Before the main feature, we will be screening the short Paradiso (2018), directed by Tim Offredi.

Paradiso is a cinematic exploration of the site of a now-defunct cinema in Atina, Italy. Across the course of a single day, the film observes a space suspended in a state of dormancy and decay, attempting to capture the essence of a place still bearing the traces and presence of its former life as a site of collective experience, where lives played out within its walls and on the screen.

The film explores how spaces become imbued with history, and how cinema and the image can become a means of connecting with memory, identity and place. Rooted in the filmmaker’s family connection to Atina, Paradiso is also a love letter to the space of cinema itself.
events.excerpt: A filmmaker recalls his childhood in a Sicilian village, where his love of cinema and friendship with a projectionist shaped his life and dreams.

events.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966) on 35mm
events.description:
The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo), 1966, Italy

Set against the turmoil of the American Civil War, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly follows three gunslingers in pursuit of buried Confederate gold. Starring Clint Eastwood, Eli Wallach, and Lee Van Cleef, the film tracks their shifting alliances as each vies for the prize. Renowned for its operatic tension and Ennio Morricone’s iconic score, it builds to one of cinema’s most legendary showdowns.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: Zombies of Mora Tau (1957) and The Vampire (1957)
events.description:
Zombies of Mora Tau opens our ‘season within a season’ look at the world of legendary producer Sam Katzman (1901-1973), whose speciality was low-budget genre films, including serials, which had disproportionately high returns for the studios and his financial backers. (See also Creature with the Atom Brain on 19 February and our double bill of The Werewolf and The Giant Claw on 12 March.)

A typical Katzman production from the late 1950s, Zombies of Mora Tau features a group of deep-sea divers who are in search of sunken treasure. However, the ship’s crew, who had all drowned – but, hint(!), whose bodies were never recovered – are particularly protective of their valuable cargo.

The most familiar member of the cast is Allison Hayes, a former Miss America contestant who would go on to achieve lasting B-movie fame the following year as the lead in Attack of the 50 Foot Woman.

The Vampire comes from south of the border, and stands well apart from the usual Mexican genre fare, which is generally characterised by Aztec Mummies and the wild, anything-goes wrestling adventures featuring Santo and his friends. It has a stateliness utterly lacking from those films, and is a particular surprise as it predated Hammer’s Dracula by almost eight months.

As with that film, the depiction of the count broke the Bela Lugosi mould, with the vampire being, like Christopher Lee, dashingly handsome and erudite. The film was a huge success, with a sequel, The Vampire’s Coffin, being rushed into production the following year.
events.excerpt: Zombies of Mora Tau opens our ‘season within a season’ look at the world of legendary producer Sam Katzman (1901-1973), whose speciality was low-budget genre films, and is joined by The Vampire, a stately Mexican film that predated Hammer’s Dracula by almost eight months.

events.title: El Topo (1970) on 35mm
events.description:
El Topo, 1970, Mexico

Set in a hallucinatory, brutal desert, El Topo follows a black-clad gunfighter on a quest for spiritual awakening through a series of ritual confrontations. Directed by and starring Alejandro Jodorowsky, the film traces his downfall and transformation as he seeks redemption among a community of outcasts. A striking fusion of symbolism and violence, it became a defining work of the midnight movie phenomenon.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: Creature with the Atom Brain (1955) and I Married a Monster from Outer Space (1958)
events.description:
Creature with the Atom Brain continues our ‘season within a season’ tribute to legendary producer Sam Katzman, who made hundreds of low budget films and serials from the 30s right up to the 60s.

Creature with the Atom Brain is a typical Katzman production, with the usual ‘off the wall’ premise that we at the Gothique love so much. A scientist, who has found a way to reanimate the dead, has happily accepted funding from a gangster – but is then not at all pleased when the gangster wants to use this awful secret for his own ghastly ends…

On its release in the USA, one local educational teachers’ group criticised it for being “a grotesque distortion of scientific facts”: Surely not??!

I Married a Monster from Outer Space has one of the best exploitation titles of all time – but this catch-penny title hides a surprisingly literate and thoughtful film.

On her wedding night, Marge realises that husband Bill is not the man she thought he was, and her search for the truth – with more and more townsfolk ‘turning’ as well – makes absorbing viewing.

Masked, perhaps, by the film’s low budget/sci-fi setting, the script arguably goes as close as any other from that era in articulating a woman’s expectations of her wedding night. This is definitely not your usual 50s sci-fi fare!
events.excerpt: Creature with the Atom Brain continues our ‘season within a season’ tribute to legendary producer Sam Katzman, and is teamed with the 1950’s sci-fi classic, I Married a Monster from Outer Space.

events.description:
In My Skin, (Dans ma peau), 2002, France

In My Skin marked the striking debut of Marina de Van. The film follows Esther, a woman whose recovery from injury turns into a troubling fixation on her own flesh, where sensation and suffering become dangerously intertwined. A haunting work of corporeal horror, it offers a raw, uncompromising vision of identity and control.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: The Werewolf (1956) and The Giant Claw (1957)
events.description:
Tonight’s films bring to an end our ‘season within a season’ tribute to legendary producer Sam Katzman, who made hundreds of low budget films and serials from the 30s right up to the 60s.

Most of them were ‘cheap and cheerful’, but The Werewolf has a surprisingly literate script and is far from Katzman’s usual low budget hokum. Indeed, Steven Ritch was rightly praised for his tormented role as a man who is unwittingly injected with “irradiated wolf serum” by an unscrupulous, but oddly well meaning, doctor. You’ll never guess what happens to him!

The Werewolf has also been noted as the film in which horror, which had been largely moribund in the USA since the early 1950s, began to assert itself over science-fiction.

The Giant Claw is a fitting end to Season 60. It really is the mother of all monster movies: once seen, never forgotten!

A giant bird (“as big as a battleship”, characters keep telling us) arrives from an “anti-matter” galaxy to terrorise the Earth. With our bombs, rockets and guns useless, can it be stopped?

In a final nod to this season, the special effects were originally to be handled by maestro Ray Harryhausen, who we profiled in November. But, instead, they were contracted out to a model-maker in Mexico City, who charged producer Sam Katzman a mere $50. Even so, some would say he was short-changed!!
events.excerpt: Tonight’s films bring to an end our ‘season within a season’ tribute to legendary producer Sam Katzman, who made hundreds of low budget films and serials from the 30s right up to the 60s.

Moulin Rouge!, 2001, Australia

Starring Nicole Kidman and Ewan McGregor, Moulin Rouge! traces a tragic love story unfolding within the infamous, glittering Parisian nightclub. A rush of visual splendor and heightened feeling à la Baz Luhrmann, the film blends contemporary songs with historical fantasy to craft a sumptuous cinematic experience.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.description:
The Age of Innocence, 1993, United States

The Age of Innocence tells the story of Newland Archer (Daniel Day-Lewis), whose engagement to an innocent socialite (Winona Ryder) binds him to the codes and rituals of his upbringing. With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: Gozu (2003) on 35mm
events.description:
Gozu, 2003, Japan

Moving between yakuza thriller, surrealist comedy and body horror, Gozu transforms the familiar codes of the gangster film into a delirious exploration of loyalty, identity and desire. Premiering in the Directors’ Fortnight at the Cannes Film Festival, Takashi Miike’s cult film showcases the director at his most unpredictable, pushing genre conventions towards the grotesque, the absurd and the uncanny.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

events.title: Audition (1999) on 35mm
events.description:
Audition, 1999, Japan

Takashi Miike’s Audition follows a widower who orchestrates a staged casting process to meet a potential partner. The film centers on his fascination with the soft-spoken Asami, whose true nature gradually comes into question. What begins as a restrained character piece slowly gives way to something far more disquieting, unfolding into a complex and unforgiving labyrinth of desire and illusion.

With an introduction by Leo Krenzer. Screened from a 35mm print in the Museum’s collection.

categories.name: The Laurel and Hardy Society
categories.description: The Live Ghost Tent - the London branch of the Laurel & Hardy Appreciation Society - holds its quarterly meetings which include screenings of Laurel and Hardy features and shorts, at the Cinema Museum. Entry is free to members and annual membership is available for a low price on the door. Find out about the origin the Live Ghost Tent's name on our Facebook page (opens in a new tab).
